source: Magnetic Fields and Their Sources
Magnets and moving charges make magnetic fields, measured in teslas, whose lines form closed loops.
Students think magnetic field lines begin and end on poles, the way electric field lines begin and end on charges.

In Electromagnets and Motors you saw that a current in a coil makes a magnet. That is the whole story of magnetism in one line: moving charge makes magnetic fields. A bar magnet works the same way. Its electrons spin and orbit, and in iron those tiny currents line up.

A magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is a vector at every point in space. A compass needle is a tiny magnet, and its north end points along $\vec{B}$. Field lines follow the compass: they leave a magnet's north pole and enter its south pole. Where the lines crowd together, the field is strong.
Field lines and compasses around a bar magnet. Each half of a broken magnet is a whole magnet with its own north and south poles.
Magnetic field lines are closed loops. Outside a magnet they run from N to S; inside they run from S back to N. The field is measured in teslas: $1\ \text{T} = 1\ \text{N/(A·m)}$.

Electric field lines start on positive charges and end on negative ones, because charges exist on their own. No one has ever found a magnetic "charge", a lone north or south pole. Every magnetic field comes from moving charge, and the field of a small current loop curls around and closes on itself. Add up loops and you still get closed lines. That is why cutting a magnet never isolates a pole: each piece is a complete magnet.

Thinking that field lines begin on the north pole and end on the south pole, like electric field lines on charges. Inside the magnet the lines keep going, from S to N, so every line is a loop. Check: a line that "ends" would need a magnetic charge there, and none has ever been found.
How strong is a tesla?
A tesla is a big unit. You will also see the gauss: $1\ \text{G} = 10^{-4}\ \text{T}$.
An MRI magnet makes $3.0\ \text{T}$. How many times stronger is that than Earth's field of $50\ \mu\text{T}$?
Comparing fields
About $60{,}000$ times stronger
Put both in teslas: $50\ \mu\text{T} = 50 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{T} = 5.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{T}$.
Divide: $$\frac{3.0\ \text{T}}{5.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{T}} = 6.0 \times 10^{4}.$$
The units cancel, so the answer is a pure number.
A compass's north end points toward Earth's geographic North Pole. What kind of magnetic pole lies under the Arctic?
Earth is a magnet
A magnetic south pole
Opposite poles attract, so the north end of the needle is pulled toward a south magnetic pole.
So a magnetic south pole lies near the geographic North Pole. Outside Earth, field lines run from the southern hemisphere toward the northern one.
The name "north pole" of a magnet is short for "north-seeking pole".
Earth's field looks like a bar magnet's, with a south magnetic pole under the Arctic.
